title: Given two strings that may contain the backspace character (#), determine whether they are equal after applying the backspaces. Aim for a solution with constant extra space. (LeetCode: Backspace String Compare)
shortTitle: Comparing Strings Containing Backspaces (Two Pointers from the End)
topicTitle: Given two strings that may contain the backspace character

s1_definition.profdef: Comparing backspace strings efficiently scans both strings from the end using two pointers, because a backspace affects characters to its left, so reading right to left lets you account for deletions as you go. You skip characters consumed by backspaces on each side and compare the surviving characters one at a time, achieving linear time and constant extra space without building the final strings.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine Rajesh and Priya each typed a reference code into a terminal, and the hash symbol means "delete the previous character" like a backspace key. We want to know if their final codes match. Instead of rebuilding both codes from scratch, we read each code backward from the last key pressed. Every time we hit a backspace, we remember to skip the next real character, because it got deleted. We line up the surviving characters from both codes and compare them one by one.
s1_definition.oneliner: Read from the right, let each backspace eat the next real character, and compare the survivors in lockstep.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Comparing backspace strings efficiently scans both strings from the end using two pointers, because a backspace affects characters to its left, so reading right to left lets you account for deletions as you go. You skip characters consumed by backspaces on each side and compare the surviving characters one at a time, achieving linear time and constant extra space without building the final strings.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine Rajesh and Priya each typed a reference code into a terminal, and the hash symbol means "delete the previous character" like a backspace key. We want to know if their final codes match. Instead of rebuilding both codes from scratch, we read each code backward from the last key pressed. Every time we hit a backspace, we remember to skip the next real character, because it got deleted. We line up the surviving characters from both codes and compare them one by one.

**One line to remember:** Read from the right, let each backspace eat the next real character, and compare the survivors in lockstep.

sections.s2_technical:
The easy approach builds each final string by simulating the typing with a stack or a string builder, then compares the two results. That is clear and correct but uses extra space proportional to the string length. The elegant approach uses two pointers scanning from the end with constant extra space.

We place a pointer at the end of each string. For each string we write a helper that, given the current pointer, skips backward over any characters that are deleted. The helper keeps a count of pending backspaces: when it sees a hash, it increments the skip count and moves left; when it sees a normal character but the skip count is positive, it decrements the skip count and moves left, consuming that character as deleted; and it stops when it finds a normal character with no pending backspaces, which is a surviving character. We call this helper on both strings to land each pointer on the next surviving character, then compare those two characters. If they differ, the strings are not equal. We repeat until both pointers fall off the start.

A finance usage example: suppose Rajesh typed `ab#c` and Priya typed `ad#c`. Reading from the end, both end in `c`, which survives and matches. Moving left, both hit a hash that deletes the preceding character, so the `b` in Rajesh's and the `d` in Priya's are both deleted. Both then land on `a`, which matches. Both pointers run off the start together, so the final codes are equal.

The senior-level nuance: the two strings may have different lengths and different numbers of backspaces, so the pointers rarely move in sync step for step; the skip helper is what realigns them onto surviving characters. A subtle correctness point is the loop termination: after skipping, one pointer might be off the start while the other still points at a surviving character, which means the strings differ, so the comparison must handle the case where only one pointer is still valid. The stack-based simulation is often easier to get right and is perfectly acceptable unless the interviewer explicitly asks for constant space.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India has a legacy entry terminal where operators type transaction reference codes, and the terminal records every keystroke including corrections, where a hash character represents pressing the backspace key. When reconciling two recorded keystroke logs, the system must decide whether the two operators ended up entering the same final reference code, even though their raw keystroke logs look different because of corrections.

Problem 2 — The logs can be long and the reconciliation runs on memory-constrained infrastructure, so rebuilding both final codes in memory is undesirable; a constant-space comparison that reads the logs from the end is preferred.

The code defines a `KeystrokeComparator` class with a `sameFinalCode` method that uses two end pointers and a skip helper to compare the surviving characters. A runnable demo compares two keystroke logs and logs whether the final codes match.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh's log `ab#c` and Priya's log `ad#c`, where the hash is a backspace.

Step 1: Both pointers start at the last index. For Rajesh that is the `c` at index 3, and for Priya that is the `c` at index 3. The skip helper finds no backspace there, so both land on `c`.

Step 2: The two surviving characters are `c` and `c`, which match. Both pointers move left to index 2.

Step 3: At index 2, both strings have a hash. The skip helper increments the skip count and moves left to index 1. At index 1, Rajesh has `b` and Priya has `d`, but each has a pending backspace, so those characters are consumed as deleted, and the helper moves left to index 0.

Step 4: At index 0, both have `a` with no pending backspace, so both land on `a`. The surviving characters `a` and `a` match. Both pointers move left to -1.

Step 5: Both pointers are now off the start at the same time, so the loop ends. Because every compared pair matched and both ended together, the final codes are equal.

Final output:

```
Oct 27, 2026 6:35:00 PM com.bank.recon.KeystrokeDemo main
INFO: Final codes match.
INFO: Logs 'ab#c' vs 'ad#c' produce the same code: true
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Rajesh: a b # c      Priya: a d # c
    │ read from right     │
    ▼                     ▼
  idx3 'c' survive  ==  idx3 'c' survive   MATCH
  idx2 '#' skip+1       idx2 '#' skip+1
  idx1 'b' deleted      idx1 'd' deleted
  idx0 'a' survive  ==  idx0 'a' survive   MATCH
  idx-1 end         ==  idx-1 end
    ▼
  final codes equal → true
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Comparing two strings that contain backspace characters comes down to a key observation: a backspace deletes characters to its left, so if I read each string from right to left, I can account for every deletion as I encounter it. That lets me compare the two strings using two pointers with only constant extra space, instead of rebuilding both final strings in memory.

I put a pointer at the end of each string and use a small skip helper for each side. The helper walks left while counting pending backspaces: every hash it sees adds one to the skip count, and every normal character it sees while the skip count is positive is consumed as deleted and decrements the count. The helper stops when it reaches a normal character with no pending backspaces, which is a surviving character. I call the helper on both strings to land each pointer on the next surviving character, compare those two characters, and if they ever differ the strings are not equal. I continue until both pointers fall off the start together.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this on a legacy entry terminal that recorded every keystroke, including corrections where a hash represented the backspace key. During reconciliation we had to decide whether two operators ended up entering the same final transaction reference code even though their raw keystroke logs looked different because of corrections. The logs were long and ran on memory-constrained infrastructure, so rebuilding both codes was wasteful, and the right-to-left two-pointer comparison did it in constant space.

The senior-level point I make is about the tricky termination condition. Because the two strings can have different lengths and different numbers of backspaces, the pointers almost never move in lockstep, and the skip helper is what realigns them onto surviving characters. The subtle bug is when one pointer still points at a surviving character while the other has already run off the start, which means the final codes differ in length, so my comparison explicitly handles the case where only one pointer is still valid. I also note that the stack-based simulation that rebuilds the strings is easier to get right and is perfectly fine unless constant space is specifically required.
